pos: n. and v. (thoughts and images passing in sleep; a divinely sent nocturnal revelation; rendering Hebrew chalom, Greek onar)
etymology: From the Saxon dream, which curiously meant joy or music, crossed with Old Norse draumr, a dream in the modern sense. Hebrew chalom is from a root meaning to be made whole or to be strong, perhaps from the restoring of sleep.
biblical_def: A dream in Scripture is sometimes only sleep and sometimes a genuine channel of revelation, and the Bible is careful about which is which. Joseph's dreams are true and cost him dearly: “And Joseph dreamed a dream, and he told it his brethren: and they hated him yet the more” (Genesis 37:5). Daniel tells Nebuchadnezzar plainly who is behind such things: “there is a God in heaven that revealeth secrets, and maketh known to the king Nebuchadnezzar what shall be in the latter days” (Daniel 2:28). Joel promises dreams as a mark of the outpoured Spirit — “your old men shall dream dreams, your young men shall see visions” (Joel 2:28) — a prophecy Peter declares fulfilled at Pentecost, when the Spirit was given and the canon of the New Testament began to be written. But Jeremiah sets the decisive limit, and it is severe: “The prophet that hath a dream, let him tell a dream; and he that hath my word, let him speak my word faithfully. What is the chaff to the wheat? saith the LORD” (Jeremiah 23:28). Dreams are chaff; the word is wheat. The comparison is not that dreams are false but that they are weightless beside Scripture. Jeremiah 23 is a chapter against prophets who prophesied out of their own hearts and called it revelation, and the LORD's complaint is that they steal his words from one another and say He saith.
webster_summary: Images passing in sleep; sometimes in Scripture a channel of revelation. Jeremiah 23:28 fixes the standing rule — dreams are chaff and the word is wheat — and the canon is now closed.
webster_full: DREAM, n. [Sax. dream.] The thought or series of thoughts of a person in sleep.
2. In Scripture, dreams were sometimes impressions on the mind of sleeping persons, made by divine agency, and used to foretell future events.
3. A vain fancy; a wild conceit; an unfounded suspicion.
4. DREAM, v.i. To have ideas or images in the mind, in the state of sleep.
5. To think; to imagine; as, he little dreamed of his approaching fate.
corruption_summary: Dreams are treated as a living channel of divine guidance, and modern prophets build ministries on them — against a closed canon and against Jeremiah's verdict that a dream is chaff beside the word.
corruption_paragraphs: The New Apostolic Reformation and the wider charismatic stream have restored the dream to a place Scripture does not give it, treating nocturnal impressions as words from God to be acted on, published, and obeyed. Two things forbid this. First, the canon is closed; God has spoken finally in his Son (Hebrews 1:1-2), and the sufficiency of Scripture means no further revelation is needed or promised for faith and life. Second, Jeremiah 23 addresses exactly this practice and calls it chaff. The prophets he condemns were not conscious frauds in every case; they told what they had genuinely dreamed and attached the LORD's name to it. That is the error — not the dreaming, but the labelling. Joel's prophecy is not a standing warrant either: Peter applies it to Pentecost, the era in which God completed his revelation, not to a permanent office of dreamers.

The principle to recover is the wheat. Jeremiah does not tell the dreamer to be silent; he tells him to call his dream a dream, and to let the man who has God's word speak that word faithfully. A Christian may dream vividly and think about it as much as he likes. What he may not do is bind another conscience with it, because the only thing that binds a conscience absolutely is Scripture. The practical test is simple and old: whatever is true in an impression is already in the word, and whatever is not in the word has no authority however vivid the night was.
roots_summary: Hebrew chalom is a dream, true or false; chalam, to dream. Greek onar is a dream, used of Joseph in Matthew 1-2; enupnion is that seen in sleep.
roots_lines: Hebrew chalom (H2472) — a dream; used of Joseph's, Pharaoh's, and the false prophets' alike.
Hebrew chalam (H2492) — to dream; also to be made healthy or strong.
Hebrew chizzayon (H2384) — a vision, especially of the night; paired with dream in Daniel 2:28.
Greek onar (G3677) — a dream; the word of Joseph's four dreams in Matthew.
Greek enupnion (G1798) — that which appears in sleep; the word quoted from Joel at Pentecost.

Of God as the revealer behind them: there is a God in heaven that revealeth secrets (Daniel 2:28).
Of the standing limit: what is the chaff to the wheat? saith the LORD (Jeremiah 23:28).

pos: n. (the explanation of a thing obscure; the rendering of one tongue into another; rendering Hebrew pithron, Greek hermeneia and epilusis)
etymology: From the Latin interpretatio, from interpres, an agent between parties, a translator. Greek hermeneia is from Hermes, the messenger of the Greek gods — the interpreter stands between a message and its hearer and adds nothing of his own.
biblical_def: Interpretation in Scripture is chiefly the unlocking of what God has said, and the Bible attributes the key to God rather than to the interpreter. Joseph states the doctrine in a prison: told that two men had dreamed and there was no interpreter, he answers, “Do not interpretations belong to God? tell me them, I pray you” (Genesis 40:8). He then interprets, but the ownership has been settled first. Before Pharaoh he is blunter still: “It is not in me: God shall give Pharaoh an answer of peace” (Genesis 41:16). Daniel takes the same ground, denying that the secret was revealed to him “for any wisdom that I have more than any living” (Daniel 2:30). The pattern is uniform: the men in Scripture most gifted at interpretation are the quickest to disclaim the gift as their own. In the New Testament interpretation appears as a distinct gift of the Spirit given to the assembly, “to another the interpretation of tongues” (1 Corinthians 12:10) — and Paul's whole argument in chapter 14 is that without it, tongues must be silent, because the assembly is built by what it understands. Peter adds the governing rule for Scripture itself: no prophecy of the Scripture is of any private interpretation (2 Peter 1:20). The Bible is not a text each man unlocks privately; it interprets itself, Scripture by Scripture.
webster_summary: The explanation of what is obscure. Scripture assigns the key to God, not the interpreter — do not interpretations belong to God? — and forbids private interpretation of prophecy.
webster_full: INTERPRETATION, n. [L. interpretatio.] The act of interpreting; explanation of what is unintelligible or not understood.
2. The sense given by an interpreter; exposition.
3. The power of explaining; as, to another the interpretation of tongues, 1 Cor. 12.
4. The act of translating from one language into another.
5. In a good or bad sense; as, to put a favorable interpretation on a man's conduct.
corruption_summary: Every reader is made his own final authority — what the text means to me — while the church's confessions and the rule that Scripture interprets Scripture are set aside as constraints on the individual.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern instinct is that a text has as many valid meanings as it has readers, and religious speech has absorbed it wholesale: what matters is what the passage means to you. Peter forecloses it. No prophecy of Scripture is of any private interpretation, because the men who wrote it did not speak by the will of man but were moved by the Holy Ghost (2 Peter 1:20-21). A text authored by one Spirit has one intended sense, and the reader's task is to find it, not to furnish it. This is why the Reformers insisted that Scripture interprets Scripture, that the clear governs the obscure, and that the analogy of faith keeps a reader from building a doctrine on a single hard verse.

The principle to recover is the interpreter's emptiness. It is not in me (Genesis 41:16) is the right posture for anyone who handles the word, and it stands against two opposite failures: the man who thinks a text yields to cleverness, and the man who thinks it yields to nothing. Confessions are the church's corporate answer to the same danger — the 1689 London Baptist Confession is a subordinate standard, binding on those who receive it and always under Scripture, and its use is precisely to keep interpretation from becoming private. A reader who has never let the church's settled reading correct him has not escaped authority; he has only reduced it to one man.
roots_summary: Hebrew pithron is the interpretation of a dream, from pathar, to open. Greek hermeneia is translation or explanation; epilusis, an unloosing, is Peter's word in 2 Peter 1:20.
roots_lines: Hebrew pithron (H6623) — interpretation, chiefly of dreams; from pathar, to open or unfold.
Hebrew pesher (H6591) — interpretation; the Aramaic term used through Daniel 2 and 5.
Greek hermeneia (G2058) — interpretation, translation; the gift of 1 Corinthians 12:10.
Greek epilusis (G1955) — an unloosing, a solution; private interpretation, 2 Peter 1:20.
Greek diermeneuo (G1329) — to interpret thoroughly; the Lord expounded the Scriptures on the Emmaus road.
usage: Of the ownership of interpretation: do not interpretations belong to God? (Genesis 40:8).

pos: n. and a. (that which is hidden or concealed; God's hidden counsel; rendering Hebrew sod and sathar, Greek kruptos)
etymology: From the Latin secretus, set apart, from secerno, to separate. Hebrew sod is richer than the English: it means both a confidential circle of counsellors and the counsel spoken there, so that God's sod is his private council and its business.
biblical_def: Scripture divides all knowledge with one verse: “The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever, that we may do all the words of this law” (Deuteronomy 29:29). Two estates are marked out, and the boundary is not a temporary one; God keeps some things and gives others, and what he gives is given with a purpose — that we may do. The revealed is for obedience, not for speculation. Yet secrecy in God is not coldness. “The secret of the LORD is with them that fear him; and he will shew them his covenant” (Psalm 25:14) — sod here is intimacy, the counsel a man shares with friends, and the condition is fear rather than cleverness. Amos states the prophetic principle: “Surely the Lord GOD will do nothing, but he revealeth his secret unto his servants the prophets” (Amos 3:7). And our Lord turns the word toward the devotional life: “pray to thy Father which is in secret; and thy Father which seeth in secret shall reward thee openly” (Matthew 6:6). The same God whose hidden counsels are none of our business is a Father who keeps company in a shut room. Secrecy in Scripture therefore protects two things at once: God's freedom from our audit, and the believer's piety from an audience.
webster_summary: That which is hidden. Deuteronomy 29:29 divides all knowledge into what God keeps and what he gives for obedience; Psalm 25:14 makes his secret an intimacy granted to those who fear him.
webster_full: SECRET, a. [L. secretus, from secerno, to separate.] Properly, separate; hence, hid; concealed from the notice or knowledge of all persons except the individual concerned.
2. Unseen; private; secluded; being in retirement.
3. Removed from sight; private; as a secret place.
4. SECRET, n. Something studiously concealed. A talebearer revealeth secrets, Prov. 11.
5. A thing not discovered, and therefore unknown; as the secrets of nature.
corruption_summary: Deuteronomy 29:29 is trespassed from both sides — by speculation that demands God explain his decrees, and by a false modesty that treats the revealed things as too mysterious to obey.
corruption_paragraphs: The doctrine of election draws the first error out of hiding. Told that God chooses according to his good pleasure and not on foreseen faith, men demand the reason behind the choice, and when it is not supplied they conclude the doctrine is unjust. Deuteronomy 29:29 answers before the question is asked: the secret things belong to the LORD. Paul answers the same objection the same way — Nay but, O man, who art thou that repliest against God? (Romans 9:20) — not because there is no answer but because it is not ours. The second error works in reverse, and hides behind humility: a man calls the clear commands mysterious to avoid keeping them. But the verse gives revelation a purpose, that we may do all the words of this law. What God has spoken plainly he expects to be obeyed plainly.

The principle to recover is that God's hiddenness and his intimacy are not in competition. The same book that forbids prying into his decrees says his sod — his private counsel — is with them that fear him. The Christian is not shut out of God's company; he is shut out of God's ledger. And Matthew 6:6 shows where the intimacy is actually enjoyed: not in the discovery of hidden things, but in a closed door and an unwitnessed prayer, which is the one secret God rewards openly.
roots_summary: Hebrew sod is a confidential circle and the counsel spoken in it; sathar, to hide. Greek kruptos is hidden, and musterion a secret now disclosed.
roots_lines: Hebrew sod (H5475) — a council of friends, and the intimate counsel spoken there; Psalm 25:14.
Hebrew sathar (H5641) — to hide, conceal; the root of the secret things of Deuteronomy 29:29.

Greek kruptos (G2927) — hidden, concealed; thy Father which seeth in secret.
Greek musterion (G3466) — a mystery, a secret kept and then revealed; not an unknowable thing but a disclosed one.

Of intimacy granted to the fearing: the secret of the LORD is with them that fear him (Psalm 25:14).
Of unwitnessed prayer: pray to thy Father which is in secret (Matthew 6:6).

pos: n. and v. (a target aimed at; a sign set upon a person or thing; rendering Hebrew tav and mattara, Greek skopos and stigma)
etymology: From the Saxon mearc, a boundary, sign, or limit — the same root as march, a border territory. The two English senses, a target and a brand, both descend from the idea of something set to be noticed.
biblical_def: Mark runs along two lines in the Authorized Version. The first is a target. “I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 3:14) — Greek skopos, the thing a runner fixes his eye on, the same root that gives us scope. Jonathan uses it in the plain sense, shooting arrows “as though I shot at a mark” (1 Samuel 20:20). Paul's image is exact: a runner who looks anywhere but at the mark loses the line, and the Christian life has one fixed point of attention. The second line is a sign set upon a person, and it cuts both ways. In Ezekiel the man with the writer's inkhorn is sent to “set a mark upon the foreheads of the men that sigh and that cry for all the abominations that be done in the midst thereof” (Ezekiel 9:4) — the marked are those grieved by the sin of their own city, and the mark preserves them when judgment falls. Paul bears a different kind: “I bear in my body the marks of the Lord Jesus” (Galatians 6:17), Greek stigmata, the brand burned on a slave to show whose he was. Scarred by stoning and scourging, Paul claims those wounds as ownership papers. The two lines meet in the sufferer, who finds himself the target: “He hath bent his bow, and set me as a mark for the arrow” (Lamentations 3:12) — and it is worth noting where that verse sits, some twenty lines before his compassions fail not; they are new every morning. Against all these stands the counterfeit mark of Revelation, by which a later power brands its own.
webster_summary: A target, and a sign set upon a person. Paul presses toward the mark and bears the slave-brand of Christ; Ezekiel's mark preserves those who grieve over their city's sin.
webster_full: MARK, n. [Sax. mearc, a bound, limit, sign.] A visible line, character or impression, made on any thing.
2. A character made by a person who cannot write his name, and intended as a substitute for it.
3. Any thing set up to be aimed at; hence, the object of aim, or that to which the mind is directed.
4. A distinguishing badge or sign; as the marks of a good man.
5. MARK, v.t. To observe; to note; to take notice of; as, mark my words.
corruption_summary: The mark of Ezekiel 9 — set on those who grieve over the sin of their own people — is little known, while endless speculation attaches to the mark of Revelation and identifies it with each generation's new technology.
corruption_paragraphs: A vast popular literature, most of it dispensational in framework, has fixed the church's attention on identifying the mark of the beast with whatever means of commerce is newest — a barcode, a chip, a payment system — and each identification has aged badly. The framework itself is a nineteenth-century novelty, unknown to any Reformation confession, and the confidence with which it dates and diagrams the last things exceeds what Scripture gives. Meanwhile Ezekiel 9:4, which is about a mark actually set on real people by God, goes largely unpreached. There the marked are not those who escaped the culture but those who sigh and cry over the abominations done in the midst of their own city — men who did not merely disapprove of their nation's sin but grieved over it.

The principle to recover is Paul's single point of attention. I press toward the mark (Philippians 3:14) is written by a man who has just listed everything he might have looked at instead — his pedigree, his tribe, his blameless record in the law — and counted it loss. A runner cannot watch two things. The marks he does accept are the ones burned into his body by opposition, and he names them as a slave names his master's brand: they settle whose he is, and they end the argument.
roots_summary: Hebrew tav is a mark or signature, the last letter of the alphabet, set on the foreheads in Ezekiel 9. Greek skopos is a goal watched; stigma, a brand burned on a slave.

Hebrew mattara (H4307) — a target, a mark to shoot at; Jonathan's arrows in 1 Samuel 20.
Greek skopos (G4649) — a goal fixed on by the eye; the mark of Philippians 3:14.
Greek stigma (G4742) — a brand pricked or burned on a slave; the marks of the Lord Jesus.

Of a mark of preservation on mourners: set a mark upon the foreheads of the men that sigh and that cry (Ezekiel 9:4).

pos: n. and v. (regard, deference; partiality shown to persons; rendering Hebrew nasa panim, to lift the face, Greek prosopolepsia)
etymology: From the Latin respicio, to look back at, to have regard to. The biblical idiom behind it is physical: to accept the face of a man, that is, to lift up his countenance in court — to judge by who is standing before you rather than by what is true.
biblical_def: Respect in the Authorized Version usually appears in the phrase respect of persons, and it names a specific sin: deciding a matter by the standing of the man rather than by the merits of the case. Of God it is denied absolutely. Moses says the LORD “regardeth not persons, nor taketh reward” (Deuteronomy 10:17), and the same verse first calls him God of gods and Lord of lords — his impartiality is a function of his greatness, since only the needy can be bought. Peter states it as the discovery that opened the gospel to the nations: “Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons” (Acts 10:34). James forbids it in the assembly, and the setting is a seating arrangement: “have not the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, with respect of persons” (James 2:1), then describes a rich man given the good seat and a poor man told to stand. To hold the faith with respect of persons is, James says, a contradiction in terms. But the word has a second and wholly good use: Moses, refusing Egypt, is commended because “he had respect unto the recompence of the reward” (Hebrews 11:26) — here it means to look toward a thing and weigh it. Regard directed at God's promise is faith; regard directed at a man's rank is sin.
webster_summary: Regard. Directed at God's promise it is faith (Hebrews 11:26); directed at a man's rank it is the sin of respect of persons, denied of God and forbidden in the assembly.
webster_full: RESPECT, v.t. [L. respicio, to look back, to regard.] To regard; to have regard to in design or purpose.
2. To have regard to, in relation or connection; to relate to.
3. To view or consider with some degree of reverence; to esteem as possessed of real worth.
4. RESPECT, n. Regard; attention.
5. Respect of persons, partiality; undue bias to a person's interest, from regard to his rank or station.
corruption_summary: Impartiality is redefined as an obligation to weight judgments by group identity, so that the very partiality James forbids is reintroduced as justice — while ordinary deference to office is dismissed as servility.
corruption_paragraphs:
The frameworks that sort men into oppressor and oppressed by race or class claim to be correcting partiality, and in fact reinstate it. James 2 does not say the poor man should be given the good seat and the rich man told to stand; it says the assembly must not seat men by their coats at all. Scripture's own categories are different in kind — the widow, the orphan, the stranger, and the poor are named as those God defends because they lack a defender in court, not as a class whose claims are automatically superior. Leviticus 19:15 makes this explicit by forbidding the error in both directions: thou shalt not respect the person of the poor, nor honour the person of the mighty. An anthropology built on one-in-Adam and one-in-Christ has no room for a permanent hierarchy of moral standing by group. 

The opposite abuse also runs. Because deference is now suspect, honour owed to parents, magistrates, and elders is treated as mere social conditioning. Scripture commands that honour plainly, and a man may honour an office wholeheartedly while refusing to be bought by the man who holds it.

The principle to recover is that impartiality is a divine attribute before it is a human duty. God regardeth not persons, nor taketh reward (Deuteronomy 10:17), and every command to judge without respect of persons is grounded in imitation of him. This is also why Peter's discovery in Acts 10 was so large. It was not a new sentiment about human equality; it was the recognition that a God who does not accept faces will not accept a Jewish face over a Roman one, and that the gospel therefore had to go to Cornelius's house that afternoon.
roots_summary: Hebrew idiom nasa panim is to lift or accept the face — to show partiality. Greek prosopolepsia is literally face-receiving; apoblepo in Hebrews 11:26 is to look away toward a thing.
roots_lines: Hebrew nasa panim (H5375 with H6440) — to lift up the face, to accept a person; the idiom of partiality.
Hebrew nakar (H5234) — to regard, to discriminate; used in the command not to respect persons in judgment.
Greek prosopolepsia (G4382) — respect of persons, face-receiving; James 2:1.
Greek prosopoleptes (G4381) — a respecter of persons; the term Peter denies of God in Acts 10:34.
Greek apoblepo (G578) — to look away from all else toward one thing; Moses' respect unto the reward.

Of partiality forbidden in the assembly: have not the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ… with respect of persons (James 2:1).
Of regard directed rightly: he had respect unto the recompence of the reward (Hebrews 11:26).

Esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures in Egypt: for he had respect unto the recompence of the reward.

pos: n. pl. (deeds, practices, the whole course of a man's or a people's conduct; rendering Hebrew maalal and alilah)
etymology: From do, Saxon don. Hebrew maalal is from alal, to act or work upon, and denotes practices rather than single acts — which is why the prophets so often pair it with ways: a man's doings are his habits made visible.
biblical_def: Doings is the prophets' word for a settled course of conduct, and it is nearly always used where God is weighing a people rather than an individual act. Hosea states the principle of exact recompense: “I will punish them for their ways, and reward them their doings” (Hosea 4:9) — and the clause before it, like people, like priest, refuses the clergy any exemption. Jeremiah names them as the reason judgment is coming on the house of David: God's fury will burn “because of the evil of your doings” (Jeremiah 21:12), in a verse whose first half commands the king to execute judgment in the morning and deliver the spoiled out of the oppressor's hand. What God indicts is not merely private vice but a court that would not do justice. Micah puts the sharp question to a people who resented such preaching: “is the spirit of the LORD straitened? are these his doings?” (Micah 2:7) — that is, is the fault in God or in you? Ezekiel shows what grace produces when it comes: “Then shall ye remember your own evil ways, and your doings that were not good, and shall lothe yourselves in your own sight” (Ezekiel 36:31), and the order is decisive. The self-loathing comes after the promised new heart, not before it. And the word serves for God's own acts too: “declare among the people his doings” (Psalm 9:11).
webster_summary: Deeds and settled practices. The prophets weigh a people by their doings, God rewards them exactly, and Ezekiel shows true shame for them arriving after the new heart, not before it.
webster_full: DOINGS, n. plu. Things done; transactions; feats; actions, good or bad.
2. Conduct; behavior; course of life.
3. Stir; bustle; as, here is fine doings.
4. In Scripture, the practices of a people considered as a whole; as, the evil of your doings, Jer. 21.
5. Also of God's acts; declare among the people his doings, Ps. 9.
corruption_summary: Conduct is separated from worship, so that a people's doings are treated as a private matter beside their profession — the exact division Hosea and Jeremiah were sent to destroy.
corruption_paragraphs: The prophets confront a religion in good working order. The feasts were kept, the priesthood functioned, the temple stood — and God pronounced against the nation because of its doings: false weights, a court that would not deliver the oppressed, and priests no better than the people they served. Hosea's like people, like priest forecloses the modern instinct that leadership failure is a separate category from congregational compromise; the two rise and fall together. Wherever a church becomes exact about doctrine and vague about practice, or exact about practice and vague about doctrine, the prophets have something to say, and Micah's question waits at the end of it: are these his doings? The fault is never in God.

The principle to recover is Ezekiel's order. God says he will sprinkle clean water, give a new heart, take away the stony heart, put his Spirit within — and then shall ye remember your own evil ways and lothe yourselves (Ezekiel 36:25-31). Repentance of this depth is a fruit of regeneration, not a qualification for it. This is the monergistic pattern the whole Reformed doctrine of conversion rests on: the new heart is given, and the loathing of the old doings follows. A man who waits until he is sufficiently ashamed before he comes to Christ has the order backwards and will wait for ever.
roots_summary: Hebrew maalal is a deed or practice, usually in the plural and usually under judgment; alilah is an act or exploit, used of God's doings as well as man's.
roots_lines: Hebrew maalal (H4611) — doings, practices; the prophets' standard term for a settled course of conduct.

pos: n. (that which remains after a part is taken; the remainder of a people; rendering Hebrew shear and yether)
etymology: From the Latin residuum, from resideo, to remain behind, to settle. In the KJV it overlaps with remnant, but tends toward the plain arithmetic of what is left over rather than the theological weight of a preserved seed.
biblical_def: Residue is what is left when the rest has been taken, and Scripture uses it with a striking range. Isaiah employs it to expose the absurdity of idolatry: a man cuts a tree, burns half for warmth and bakes bread on the coals, and “the residue thereof he maketh a god, even his graven image: he falleth down unto it, and worshippeth it” (Isaiah 44:17). The whole argument is in the word. The god is the offcut — the leftover of a fire — and a man who would not think twice about the first half kneels to the second. Haggai uses it of a people: the prophet is sent to Zerubbabel, to Joshua the high priest, “and to the residue of the people” (Haggai 2:2), a small remainder returned from exile, discouraged by a house so much poorer than the first. Jeremiah uses it under judgment: death shall be chosen rather than life “by all the residue of them that remain of this evil family” (Jeremiah 8:3). And Malachi puts it to a purpose that governs marriage. Asking why God made one wife for one man when he had the power to make more, the prophet answers: “And did not he make one? Yet had he the residue of the spirit. And wherefore one? That he might seek a godly seed” (Malachi 2:15). God had spirit to spare and deliberately did not spend it. Monogamy is not a limit on his resources but a design for godly children.
webster_summary: What remains when the rest is taken. Isaiah makes an idol the offcut of a cooking fire; Malachi grounds one-man-one-woman marriage in a God who had the residue of the spirit and made one anyway.
webster_full: RESIDUE, n. [L. residuum, from resideo, to remain.] That which remains after a part is taken, separated, removed or designated.
2. The remainder; the rest; that which is left.
3. In law, the part of an estate which remains after payment of debts and legacies.
4. In chemistry, that which remains of a body after the separation of a part.
5. In Scripture, the remainder of a people; the residue of the people, Hag. 2.
corruption_summary: Malachi 2:15 is a chief text for the creational form of marriage, and it is routinely passed over — while the patriarchal polygamy Scripture records is treated as though Scripture endorsed it.
corruption_paragraphs: A common argument against the one-man-one-woman standard runs from the narratives: Abraham, Jacob, David, and Solomon had more than one wife, and the Bible does not always stop to condemn it. But the Bible never commends it either, and it takes pains to show what it produced — Hagar and Sarah, Leah and Rachel, and a king whose wives turned away his heart. Malachi answers the argument at its root by going behind the narratives to the creation: God made one, and he had the residue of the spirit — he could have made more and did not — and the stated purpose was a godly seed. The form of marriage is therefore not a cultural accident of the ancient near east but a design aimed at children raised in the fear of God, which is why Christ grounds the whole law of marriage in what was so from the beginning (Matthew 19:4-6).

The principle to recover is what Malachi does with that doctrine, since he does not leave it abstract. The verse ends: therefore take heed to your spirit, and let none deal treacherously against the wife of his youth. The doctrine of creational marriage lands as a warning to husbands about faithfulness to an aging wife, which is the form the temptation actually takes. Haggai's use is worth setting beside it. A residue is a small and discouraged thing, and God sent his prophet to that remainder with a promise about a house whose latter glory would exceed the first.
roots_summary: Hebrew shear is a remainder or remnant, from shaar, to be left over; yether is the rest or excess. Greek kataloipos is the residue of men in Acts 15:17.
roots_lines: Hebrew shear (H7605) — a remainder, a remnant; what survives when the rest is taken away.
Hebrew yether (H3499) — the rest, the excess, that which is over and above.
Hebrew shaar (H7604) — to remain, to be left; the verb behind the doctrine of the remnant.
Hebrew ruach (H7307) — spirit, breath; the residue of the spirit God did not spend, Malachi 2:15.
Greek kataloipos (G2645) — remaining, left over; the residue of men that might seek after the Lord.
usage: Of an idol made from an offcut: the residue thereof he maketh a god (Isaiah 44:17).
Of a small returned people: and to the residue of the people (Haggai 2:2).
Of the ground of monogamy: yet had he the residue of the spirit. And wherefore one? (Malachi 2:15).

Jeremiah 8:3

pos: n. (a flowing out; offspring; the outcome of a matter; rendering Hebrew zob and totsaah, Greek rhusis)
etymology: From Old French issue, a going out, from Latin exeo, to go forth. Every English sense — a discharge, a man's offspring, the outcome of an affair — keeps the root idea of something that comes forth from a source.
biblical_def: Issue is what comes forth, and Scripture uses it in three registers that turn out to be one. It is a bodily discharge rendering a person ceremonially unclean: “When any man hath a running issue out of his flesh, because of his issue he is unclean” (Leviticus 15:2). The law of Leviticus 15 is not squeamishness; it teaches by the body that what comes out of a man defiles him, and it sets up our Lord's later declaration that defilement is a matter of what proceeds from the heart. Against that background stands the woman “which was diseased with an issue of blood twelve years” (Matthew 9:20). Twelve years unclean, barred from the assembly and from touch, she comes behind him and touches the hem of his garment — and the uncleanness does not pass to him; the healing passes to her. That is the gospel in a single gesture. Proverbs uses the word for the heart's output: “Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life” (Proverbs 4:23). The heart is the spring, and everything downstream takes its character from it — which is why the command is to guard the source rather than to police the streams. And the Psalter reserves the last outcome to God: “unto GOD the Lord belong the issues from death” (Psalm 68:20). The ways out of death are his to open.
webster_summary: That which flows or comes forth. Leviticus makes an issue defiling, Christ reverses the flow at the hem of his garment, Proverbs makes the heart the spring of life's issues, and the exits from death belong to God.
webster_full: ISSUE, n. ish'u. [Fr. issue, from issir, L. exeo, to go out.] The act of passing or flowing out; a moving out of any inclosed place.
2. A flowing out; a discharge; as an issue of blood.
3. Progeny; a child or children; offspring.
4. Event; consequence; end; ultimate result; as the issue of an affair.
5. ISSUE, v.i. To pass or flow out; to run out, as from any inclosed place.
corruption_summary: Behaviour is managed at the outlet rather than the source, against Proverbs 4:23 — and the ceremonial laws of Leviticus 15 are dismissed as primitive rather than read as instruction in defilement.
corruption_paragraphs: Almost every scheme of self-improvement works downstream: it identifies conduct to be modified and applies technique to the modifying. Proverbs 4:23 puts the labour somewhere else. Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life — the streams are named as issues precisely to send the reader back to the spring. Our Lord argues the same way when he lists what proceeds out of the heart and calls those things the defilement (Matthew 15:19-20). This is why regeneration, and not reformation, is the Christian answer to sin. A new heart changes what comes forth; a managed exterior only filters it, and filters fail.

The principle to recover is what happened at the hem. Under the law, contact with an issue of blood transmitted uncleanness to the one touched — that was the settled expectation, and it is why the woman came from behind and in silence. When she touched Christ the traffic ran the other way: she was made whole, and he was not defiled. It is a small enacted parable of the atonement, in which the holy One takes contact with the unclean and the uncleanness does not stick to him but is destroyed. And it points forward to Psalm 68:20, since the issues from death belong to the same Lord, who opened one for himself and therefore for her.
roots_summary: Hebrew zob is a flux or discharge, from zub, to flow; totsaah is an outgoing or source. Greek rhusis is a flowing, the word of the woman's issue of blood.

Hebrew totsaah (H8444) — an outgoing, a source or border; the issues of life in Proverbs 4:23.
Hebrew tsaetsa (H6631) — offspring, that which issues from a man; his issue after him.

pos: a. (later; the second of two; belonging to the end; rendering Hebrew acharon, Greek husteros)
etymology: From the Saxon laetra, the comparative of laet, late — the older comparative preserved beside the newer later. English has since divided the two, keeping latter for the second of a pair and for what belongs to the end.
biblical_def: Latter in the Authorized Version points to the end of something, and four uses carry great weight. Job, in the oldest book of the canon, states the resurrection hope: “For I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth” (Job 19:25). The redeemer is alive now and will stand then, upon this earth — a bodily hope, not a flight from matter. Haggai speaks to the discouraged builders of the second temple: “The glory of this latter house shall be greater than of the former… and in this place will I give peace” (Haggai 2:9). Measured in cedar and gold the second house was the poorer; measured by the One who would walk in its courts, it was incomparably greater. Paul warns of a corruption belonging to the end: “in the latter times some shall depart from the faith, giving heed to seducing spirits, and doctrines of devils” (1 Timothy 4:1) — and the mechanism named is doctrinal, a departure by teaching rather than by persecution. Proverbs brings the word down to the ordinary: “Hear counsel, and receive instruction, that thou mayest be wise in thy latter end” (Proverbs 19:20). A man's latter end is the part of his life he cannot revise, and the wisdom it will display is being accumulated now, by whether he takes correction.
webster_summary: Later; the second of two; belonging to the end. Job's redeemer stands at the latter day, Haggai's latter house exceeds the former, and Proverbs makes a man's latter end the sum of the counsel he took.
webster_full: LATTER, a. [a corruption of later, the comparative degree of late.] Coming or happening after something else; opposed to former.
2. Mentioned the last of two; opposed to former.
3. Modern; lately done or past; as in these latter ages.
4. LATTER-END, n. The end or conclusion; the close of life.
5. LATTER-MATH, n. The latter mowing; that which is mowed after the first crop.
corruption_summary: The latter days are turned into a chart of dates and world events, chiefly by a nineteenth-century scheme no Reformation confession knew — while Paul's own warning about the latter times, which is doctrinal, goes unheeded.
corruption_paragraphs: Dispensational premillennialism, systematised by Darby and popularised by the Scofield Bible, has made the latter days an object of calculation: charts, timetables, and a sequence of events fitted to each generation's headlines. It is a novelty. No Reformation confession contains it, and the wider Reformed tradition has held amillennial, postmillennial, and historic premillennial positions without needing it. Its practical damage is that it directs attention outward, to the news, when Paul directs it inward, to doctrine. His warning in 1 Timothy 4:1 is not about geopolitics; it is that some shall depart from the faith by giving heed to seducing spirits and doctrines of devils, and the remedy he prescribes two verses on is the ministry of good doctrine and the word of God received with thanksgiving.

The principle to recover is Haggai's measure of glory. The men who wept at the second temple's foundation were right about the cedar and wrong about the glory, because glory was going to be measured by a Person walking in those courts rather than by the building's inventory. That is the standing correction to every assessment of the church's latter state made by counting visible resources. It also fits Job, who had no temple and no visible ground of confidence at all, and who nonetheless knew that his redeemer lived and would stand at the latter day upon the earth.
roots_summary: Hebrew acharon is the last or hindmost, from achar, behind. Greek husteros is later, and eschatos last — the root of eschatology.
roots_lines: Hebrew acharon (H314) — last, latter, hindmost; the latter day of Job 19:25.
Hebrew acharith (H319) — the after-part, the end, the latter end of a man or a nation.
Hebrew malqosh (H4456) — the latter rain, the spring rain that fills the ear before harvest.
Greek husteros (G5306) — latter, later; in the latter times, 1 Timothy 4:1.
Greek eschatos (G2078) — last, final; the root of the word eschatology.
usage: Of the resurrection hope: he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth (Job 19:25).
Of glory not measured by materials: the glory of this latter house shall be greater than of the former (Haggai 2:9).
Of doctrinal departure at the end: in the latter times some shall depart from the faith (1 Timothy 4:1).

pos: n. (that by which an end is accomplished; instrument, method; chiefly in the KJV in the phrases by no means and by all means)
etymology: From Old French meien, from Latin medianus, middle — a means is what stands in the middle between an intention and its accomplishment. The KJV's commonest use is adverbial, in the emphatic negatives and positives.
biblical_def: Means is the middle term between a purpose and its end, and Scripture handles it in two ways that must be held together. First, in the emphatic negative, it marks what God will not do: he keeps mercy for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, “and that will by no means clear the guilty” (Exodus 34:7). That clause stands inside the great self-revelation of God's name, immediately after the mercy, and the two are not in competition — they meet at the cross, where the guilty are cleared precisely because guilt was not waived but borne. Our Lord uses the same emphatic form of the believer's safety: “nothing shall by any means hurt you” (Luke 10:19), and Paul of the last things: “Let no man deceive you by any means” (2 Thessalonians 2:3). Second, and positively, means describes the instruments God appoints for his ends. Paul's missionary rule is the classic case: “I am made all things to all men, that I might by all means save some” (1 Corinthians 9:22). This is the doctrine of means in a sentence. God has decreed the salvation of his elect, and he has decreed the preaching, the travel, the flexibility, and the self-denial by which they will be saved. Election never makes the means unnecessary; it is precisely what guarantees they will not be wasted.
webster_summary: That by which an end is accomplished. God will by no means clear the guilty, and Paul will by all means save some — the appointed instruments through which God's decree reaches its end.
webster_full: MEANS, n. plu. [from mean, middle.] That which is used to effect an object; instrument; that which is subservient to an end.
2. Income; revenue; resources; as, a man of means.
3. By all means, without fail; certainly; at all events.
4. By no means, not at all; certainly not; not in any degree.
5. By any means, possibly; at all; as, if by any means I might attain, Phil. 3.
corruption_summary: The doctrine of election is set against the use of means, so that God's decree is treated as making evangelism, prayer, and diligence unnecessary — the old fatalist error Scripture never permits.
corruption_paragraphs: The charge that Reformed theology kills missions is as old as the theology, and it survives because the objection is easy to state and the answer requires two thoughts at once. God has chosen a people; God has also appointed how they will be gathered. The decree includes the means, and it is a confusion to imagine a decreed end floating free of the road to it. Paul is the proof, since no writer states election more strongly and none travelled further. In 1 Corinthians 9 he makes himself servant to all, becomes as a Jew to Jews and as weak to the weak, and explains it by that I might by all means save some. In Acts 18 the Lord tells him at Corinth I have much people in this city — and the effect of that assurance is not that Paul leaves but that he stays a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them.

The principle to recover is the balance inside God's own name. Exodus 34 declares him merciful, gracious, longsuffering, forgiving iniquity — and in the same breath says he will by no means clear the guilty. Any doctrine of grace that quietly drops the second clause has stopped describing the God of Scripture. Penal substitution is what holds them together: the guilty are not cleared by a waiver but by a substitute, so that God is just and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus (Romans 3:26).
roots_summary: The KJV's by no means renders emphatic Hebrew and Greek constructions of double negation; by all means renders pantos, altogether, in 1 Corinthians 9:22.
roots_lines: Hebrew infinitive absolute construction — the doubled verb of Exodus 34:7 rendered by no means clear.
Hebrew naqah (H5352) — to be clean, to acquit; the verb God says he will not do for the guilty.
Greek pantos (G3843) — altogether, by all means; Paul's missionary purpose in 1 Corinthians 9:22.
Greek ou me (G3364) — the emphatic double negative, rendered by no means and in no wise.
Greek tropos (G5158) — a manner or way; by any means in 2 Thessalonians 2:3.
usage: Of what God will not do: that will by no means clear the guilty (Exodus 34:7).
Of appointed instruments in mission: that I might by all means save some (1 Corinthians 9:22).
Of guarding against deception: let no man deceive you by any means (2 Thessalonians 2:3).
